newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Key Van der Horst holders want shares back.
newsitem.headline: Key Van der Horst holders want shares back.

text.p: Infrastructure-based Van der Horst said on Tuesday its three major shareholders had not wanted banks to sell their shares given as collateral, group managing director Michael Oxborrow said.
The engineering company said banks had to sell four to five million Van der Horst shares, pledged as collateral by its major shareholders -- Johannes Kotjo, Johnlin Yuwono and Bambang Trihatmodjo.
"They didn't want to lose them in the first place. They would like to have them back," Oxborrow told a news briefing on its financial results for the six months ended March 31, 1997.
Analysts who had attended a company briefing earlier on Tuesday told Reuters they thought the major shareholders may eventually move to buy the shares back.
"I understand there is no further danger of Kotjo's holding going below 10 percent," Oxborrow said.

He said the sale represented four to five percent of issued share capital and the shares were sold in the open market from Thursday after a failure to meet margin calls after prices fell. Van der Horst shares plummeted to a 45-month low of Singapore $1.98 on Tuesday after it reported an 84-percent plunge in interim profits to Singapore $4.14 million. News of the share sales fuelled worries of brewing corporate trouble, dealers said.
The price later recovered to finish eight cents higher at S$2.27.
Oxborrow said the share sale had reduced executive chairman Kotjo's stake to 14 percent from 19 percent. Shareholdings by Trihatmodjo and Yuwono fell by one to two percent each.
He felt the current share price was not justified as net tangible assets are now at $2.14 per share and could potentially be a dollar higher if the company's Philippines' investments were included.
Oxborrow also dismissed market rumours that banks in Singapore were not giving the company additional loans.
"I have not heard of this. No banks are seeking returns on their outstanding (loans). I'm intrigued by the rumour."
Neither did Oxborrow suspect any insider trading or attempts by potential business partners to push down the share price in an attempt for a takeover.
Oxborrow said he expected the company, which saw first half profits hit by the Indonesian election, to post a recovery in the second half of its fiscal year ending September 30, 1997.

Election fever, worsened by bureaucracy and negotiation statemate, had delayed three projects in Indonesia -- Jakarta Depot Satellite and Surabaya Depot satellite pipelines and the Samarang power plant.
"We estimated the delays in Indonesia, largely initiated by election fever, gave us a six-month blip," Oxborrow said.
Growth would come from its the three delayed projects, valued at a total of US$280 million. Positive contributions were also expected from its Enron power plant project.
However, Oxborrow warned of weaker profit margins as most of the projects it has in hand were largely completed and in the final phase of construction and procurement.

"The profitable parts of Surabaya, Jakarta projects that is engineering, consultancy have largely been completed," he said. The company has an order book worth US$380 million which would see it through to mid-1999, Oxborrow said.
Van der Horst is looking expand into the region, namely ASEAN, focussing on projects which would give faster returns and have shorter incubation periods.
It was also looking to Europe and particularly Germany for opportunities to buy high technology like power plant engineering and design capabilities, which would support the group's future expansion.
-- Singapore newsroom (65 8703080)
